summary: The note describes new local public health campaigns against tobacco use that combine traditional outreach with technology, social media, storytelling, policy advocacy, targeted community work, youth education and corporate accountability. It draws on interviews with a former tobacco executive, campaign strategists, physicians, a psychologist, a teacher and a legal advisor. It stresses the threat of vaping and dual use and says success is measured by smoking rates and a broader shift in public sentiment.
one_line: Local health organizations launch innovative anti-tobacco campaigns using social media, storytelling, AI apps, advocacy, community liaisons, education and legal accountability, as described by several experts.
key_facts: Alex Richardson, a former tobacco industry executive turned tobacco control advocate, was interviewed on September 8, 2023.
Richardson called vaping 'a modern-day Trojan horse' that has re-normalized smoking behaviors, especially among the young.
Richardson cited a rise in dual use, where people smoke traditional cigarettes and also use e-cigarettes.
Campaigns on Instagram, Twitter and TikTok, launched after September 15, 2023, aim to spread awareness and build community support for a tobacco-free world.

Lucy Thompson, a campaign strategist with the local health department, said real-life testimonials work better than statistics, such as a former smoker with heart disease at 35; she was interviewed on September 22.
Stories are broadcast across podcasts and local talk shows.
Dr. Martin Green, a physician and anti-tobacco advocate, pushes public engagement for stricter regulation of tobacco sales and marketing by exposing the industry's manipulative tactics.

Dr. Emily Watson, a clinical psychologist, said AI-based apps provide personalized quit-plans, track progress, send motivational messages and connect users with support groups (conversation on October 4).
Dr. Raj Patel, who leads a community health initiative, said cultural liaisons from within high-risk communities communicate tobacco risks respectfully (briefing on October 12).
Educational programs in schools and universities were revamped in late 2023 to explain the science of nicotine addiction and the social factors behind smoking uptake.
Juliet Sanchez, a high school health teacher, said lessons show how smoking affects health, environment, social lives and futures.
Ben Choi, a public health legal advisor, said document exposés and legal battles show corporate culpability; he spoke in an address on September 30.
Richardson said the real victory will be a societal paradigm shift when smoking is no longer a normal part of life for anyone.
